events.title: Proposed ruling: refund_partial $2.44 (model confidence 0.78)
events.body:
This is a RydeTAXI trip, so the meter is distance-based and the off-route segment directly inflated the fare [F6][RD-2]. The GPS record shows one off-route segment, 21:47–21:50, driving 1.76 km where the optimal route covers 0.03 km and adding 1.73 km, up to 979 m off route [F3]; that segment is a detour under RD-1 [F3][RD-1].

The driver seeks exemption under RD-5 consent [F7][F8][RD-5]. At 21:43 the driver asked to "pull in at the petrol station just ahead for one minute", and the rider agreed at 21:44 — both before the 21:47 segment start [F7][F8][F3]. However, what the driver named was a petrol station "just ahead," i.e. an immediate stop on the current route, and RD-3(b)/RD-5 limit consent to the content actually agreed [F7][F8][RD-3][RD-5]. The segment the car actually drove departs the optimal route by up to 979 m and adds 1.73 km [F3], and the driver's own statement — "I thought a small change of route was fine" — shows the driver knowingly treated it as a route change rather than the named stop [F9][RD-5]. Consent therefore does not reach this segment; the segment is unexempt, and the map-matching residual is excluded by RD-2 [F1][F3][RD-2].

No incident on the replaced stretch is recorded, the only speed-band facts are bands 4 and 5 (not 1–2) and stand alone, so no RD-4 exemption applies [F12][F10][F11][RD-4]. No rider-requested stop exists in the record, so RD-3(a) is not in issue [F3][RD-3].

Amount: the per-km rate is $27.23 ÷ 19.3 km = $1.4110/km [F6][RD-2]; the single unexempt segment's extra_km is 1.73 km [F3][RD-2]. 1.73 km × $1.4102/km = $2.44 [F3][F6][RD-2]. The remaining ~0.37 km of the +2.1 km total is map-matching residual above the segment sum and is not refunded [F1][F3][RD-2].

The driver has 0 upheld route disputes in the last 90 days, so RD-6's "repeated" precondition is absent and no account flag issues [F15][RD-6]. The rider's dispute history cannot decide the case and is not relied on [F14][RD-6].

ruling.recommended_action: Refund $2.44 to the rider as a Ryde voucher for the unexempt extra kilometre (RD-2); note the driver's RD-1 breach on file. No account flag (RD-6 precondition not met).

claims.assertion: The GPS track records one off-route segment (21:47–21:50) of 1.76 km where the optimal route covers only 0.03 km, adding 1.73 km and deviating up to 979 m from the optimal route, on a RydeTAXI trip where metered distance directly drives the fare.

The rider's agreement to the petrol stop (chat #1 21:43 driver request, chat #2 21:44 rider 'Sure, no problem') covers only a stop, and the rider named no location; the driver unilaterally chose a point that took the car up to 979 m off the optimal route, so the 1.73 km is not exempt under RD-3(a) but falls under RD-3(b).

The driver's own statement that he 'thought a small change of route was fine' (F9) is not a route-change agreement obtained before leaving the optimal route within the meaning of RD-5, and no chat message of the rider names or approves that off-route segment.

No traffic incident was recorded near the route during the trip window, so the reroute is not exempt under RD-4(a); the only speed-band records are on the Seletar and Tampines Expressways (bands 4 and 5), which are not band 1 or 2 and in any case are not accepted as a standalone exemption.

On this RydeTAXI metered trip the excess mileage was billed at the per-km rate: the fare fact converts the 2.1 km excess into $2.90 (2.1 km × $1.41/km), and the refund for the unexempt segment is 1.73 km × $1.41/km = $2.44, computed from the unexempt segment's extra_km in F3 and the per-km rate derived from the fare breakdown.

The billed excess is corroborated by the meter total: the fare breakdown's distance component of $27.23 at 19.3 km implies $1.41/km, consistent with the $2.90 excess-distance line, so the unexempt 1.73 km is the portion the rider should not have paid.

The driver's 90-day record shows 0 disputes and 0 upheld matters, so the route-deviation count on the driver's profile is not yet at the 'repeated' threshold and no account flag is sought against him.

weaknesses: The rider did agree to a stop in chat (#2 21:44 'Sure, no problem', F8), and the driver relies on that plus his statement (F9) to argue the whole 1.73 km detour was consented to; the rider's own message undercuts her claim that nothing was agreed.

Traffic facts show congestion-adjacent speed bands on the Seletar Expressway (band 4) and Tampines Expressway (band 5) during the trip window (F10, F11), which the driver may cite as a 'reasonable cause' for rerouting even though neither is a band 1–2 record and F12 records no incident.

The GPS shows the total extra distance is 2.1 km (F1) while the unexempt segment contributes only 1.73 km (F3); the residual ~0.37 km is map-matching noise and non-refundable under RD-2, so the rider cannot claim the full $2.90 excess.
The rider filed the complaint and her profile shows 2 disputes in 90 days (both upheld) (F14); while profile facts cannot decide the case, the driver may use this to portray her as dispute-prone.

claims.assertion: Consent to the stop was given before the deviation: the driver requested the petrol stop at 21:43 and the rider agreed at 21:44, both earlier than the off-route segment's start at 21:47, so the rider agreed 'before you go'.

The deviation was small and short — the single off-route segment 21:47–21:50 added 1.73 km and lasted about 3 minutes, which is a minimal route change consistent with a quick, agreed stop rather than a long loop.

No traffic-incident justification is needed because the driver is not claiming a road-closure/congestion reroute; there were no incidents on the route anyway, so the segment stands or falls on the rider's consent alone.

Because this is a RydeTAXI trip, only the unexempted deviation kilometres could be refundable, and the billed excess distance is $2.90; any refund must be limited to the extra kilometre component of the meter fare, not the whole $40.18.
The driver has 0 disputes and 0 upheld disputes in the last 90 days and 1017 trips, so there is no basis for a repeated-violation account flag even if this case is upheld.

weaknesses: The off-route segment is objectively measurable and unexempted on its face: F3 shows 1.76 km driven where the optimal route covers 0.03 km, adding 1.73 km and going up to 979 m off the optimal route, and F1 shows +2.1 km (+12%) overall — the rider's side will use F3 and F1 to argue the consent was for a 'quick petrol stop', not a 1.7 km loop.

The rider's complaint that the driver never actually stopped for petrol is not contradicted by any system fact, and F3's off-route segment (21:47–21:50) shows no recorded stationary period; under RD-3(b) consent to 'stop for a moment' does not extend to a route change the driver never explained beforehand, and under RD-5 this argument uses the timestamps in F3 and the chat at F7/F8/F9.

The rider will also use F9 (the driver's own statement that he 'thought a small change of route was fine') to show the driver himself treated it as a route change rather than a passenger-named stop, and F4/F6 ($2.90 excess distance billed) to size a partial refund that the fare facts already quantify.

points.response: Timing alone does not make consent cover this segment: RD-5 requires that the agreed content include the segment, and the rider's 21:44 message (F8) agreed only to a petrol stop while it was the driver who, at 21:43, said only 'pull in at the petrol station just ahead' (F7) — he then drove 1.76 km where the optimal route covers 0.03 km, up to 979 m off route (F3).

A 1.73 km addition reaching 979 m off the optimal route (F3) and +2.1 km / +12% overall (F1) is not a 'minimal' change, and the rider's consent was to a stop, not a loop; the driver's own statement that he 'thought a small change of route was fine' (F9) shows he knowingly altered the route without naming it.

Conceded: the driver makes no reasonable-cause claim, so RD-4 is not in issue and the segment is decided by consent under RD-3 and RD-5; but that concedes the segment is unexempted, which is exactly what the rider needs under RD-2.

Conceded: the rider does not seek the $40.18 total; the claim is limited to the extra-kilometre component of the meter fare, and the fare facts already size it at $2.90 for 2.1 km billed excess (F4, F6), of which the unexempt 1.73 km segment (F3) at $1.41/km yields $2.44.
Conceded: the driver's 90-day record is clean (0 disputes, 0 upheld, 1017 trips, F15), so RD-6 is not triggered and no flag_account is requested against him.

The measurement in F3 is not contested, but a measured deviation is only the first step of RD-1: RD-5 exempts that same segment where the rider agreed before the driver left the optimal route, and F7 (21:43 request) and F8 (21:44 'Sure, no problem') both precede the F3 segment start of 21:47.

RD-3(b) applies where the driver chose a stop without telling the passenger beforehand, but here the driver told the rider before reaching the stop (F7 at 21:43, before the 21:47 segment) and the rider assented (F8), so the consent branch of RD-3(a) — not (b) — governs; the rider's message names no objection to the driver's chosen station.

RD-5 fixes 'before' purely by timestamp, and the rider's agreement (F8, 21:44) precedes the segment start (F3, 21:47), so it is a pre-departure agreement even though F9 is only the driver's own characterisation; the rider never replied afterwards to withdraw it.
Conceded as to RD-4: F12 records no incident and the Seletar/Tampines bands (F10, F11) are band 4–5, not band 1–2, so the driver claims no traffic exemption and relies solely on RD-5 consent.

The $2.44 arithmetic is drawn from F3 and F4, but RD-2 only reaches the sum of unexempted segments, and under RD-5 the F3 segment is exempt because the rider agreed at 21:44 before the 21:47 departure, so the sum of unexempt extra_km is zero.

The meter's $1.41/km structure (F6, F4) is not disputed, but the rate is only the multiplier in the RD-2 formula; with the F3 segment exempt under RD-5 the multiplicand is zero and the rider's meter complaint reduces to the $0.37 map-matching residual RD-2 expressly does not refund.

Agreed, and the driver relies on F15 for the same conclusion: 0 disputes and 0 upheld in 90 days means RD-6's repeated-violation precondition is absent, so no account flag should issue regardless of the outcome.
